prompt: According to the manual, what degrades your ability to think clearly and ride skillfully more than any other factor?
choices: Riding in heavy traffic
Bad weather and poor visibility
Alcohol and drugs
Riding an unfamiliar motorcycle
explanation: Alcohol and drugs, more than any other factor, degrade your ability to think clearly and ride skillfully.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Being in Shape to Ride)

prompt: How much alcohol can have a significant effect on your riding performance?
choices: Only enough to reach the legal limit
At least three drinks in an hour
Only hard liquor, not beer or wine
As little as one drink
explanation: As little as one drink can have a significant effect on performance. Impairment begins well before the legal limit is reached.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Being in Shape to Ride)

prompt: Compared with car drivers, what is true of motorcyclists in crashes involving alcohol or drugs?
choices: They are more likely to be killed or severely injured
They are less likely to be hurt because they can jump clear
They face about the same injury risk as car drivers
They are injured less often because they ride more slowly
explanation: Drinking and drug use are as big a problem among motorcyclists as among drivers, but motorcyclists are more likely to be killed or severely injured in a crash.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Why This Information Is Important)

prompt: When are the judgment and decision-making skills needed for riding first affected by alcohol?
choices: Only once you reach the legal limit
Only after you start to feel drunk
Long before legal limits are reached
Only if you drink on an empty stomach
explanation: Judgment and the decision-making processes needed for vehicle operation are affected long before legal limits are reached.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Alcohol and Drugs in Motorcycle Operation)

prompt: Which statement about over-the-counter and prescription drugs is correct?
choices: They are safe to ride on because a doctor or pharmacy supplied them
Only illegal drugs can affect your riding ability
They cancel out the effects of alcohol
Many have side effects that increase the risk of riding
explanation: Many over-the-counter, prescription and illegal drugs have side effects that increase the risk of riding.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Alcohol and Drugs in Motorcycle Operation)

prompt: How do the combined effects of alcohol and drugs compare with either one alone?
choices: The effects cancel each other out somewhat
The combination is more dangerous than either alone
The combination is no worse than the stronger one alone
Drugs reduce how much alcohol affects you
explanation: The combined effects of alcohol and drugs are more dangerous than either is alone.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Alcohol and Drugs in Motorcycle Operation)

prompt: How quickly does alcohol begin to affect a drinker?
choices: Within minutes, because it does not need to be digested
Only after about an hour, once it is digested
Only after you stop drinking
Not until the next drink is finished
explanation: Alcohol enters the bloodstream quickly. Unlike most foods and drinks, it does not need to be digested, and within minutes it reaches the brain.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Alcohol in the Body)

prompt: What does Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) measure?
choices: How many drinks you had in the last hour
How fast your body is digesting alcohol
The amount of alcohol in relation to blood in the body
How long alcohol stays in your stomach
explanation: BAC is the amount of alcohol in relation to blood in the body. The more alcohol in your blood, the greater the impairment.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Blood Alcohol Concentration)

prompt: Generally, how fast can the body eliminate alcohol?
choices: About two drinks per hour
About one drink per hour
About one drink every 15 minutes
About one drink every four hours
explanation: Generally, alcohol can be eliminated at a rate of almost one drink per hour, though other factors can affect how much is retained.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 41 (Blood Alcohol Concentration)

prompt: Which of these is one of the three primary factors that determine your BAC?
choices: The type of drink, such as beer or liquor
Whether you drink coffee afterward
How many years you have been riding
How fast you drink
explanation: The three primary factors are the amount of alcohol you consume, how fast you drink, and your body weight.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 42 (Blood Alcohol Concentration)

prompt: Which contains the most alcohol: a 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a mixed drink with one 1.5-ounce shot of liquor?
choices: They contain about the same amount
The mixed drink, because it has hard liquor
The 12-ounce beer, because it is the largest
The glass of wine, because wine is stronger than beer
explanation: A 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine and a mixed drink with one 1.5-ounce shot of liquor all contain the same amount of alcohol.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 42 (Blood Alcohol Concentration)

prompt: A rider drinks at a pace of one drink per hour. Which statement is true?
choices: The body removes it all, so BAC stays at zero
Riding is safe at this pace for any length of time
Alcohol may still build up, and even one drink can affect judgment
Only women are affected at this pace, not men
explanation: Alcohol may still accumulate even at one drink per hour, especially for women, and abilities and judgment can be affected by that one drink.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 42 (Blood Alcohol Concentration)

prompt: You have two drinks within one hour. At the end of that hour, how much alcohol remains in your bloodstream?
choices: None at all
About half a drink
Exactly two drinks
At least one drink
explanation: The body eliminates about one drink per hour, so if you drink two drinks in an hour, at least one drink will remain at the end of that hour.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 42 (Blood Alcohol Concentration)

prompt: Someone has seven drinks over three hours. Ignoring other factors, how much longer should they wait after the third hour before considering riding?
choices: At least one more hour
At least three more hours
At least four more hours
At least seven more hours
explanation: About three drinks are eliminated in three hours, leaving at least four drinks (7 - 3 = 4). That takes at least another four hours to eliminate.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 42 (Blood Alcohol Concentration)

prompt: A rider has four drinks over two hours. Ignoring other factors, how many drinks' worth of alcohol remain at the end of the two hours?
choices: At least two
At least one
At least three
None, if they ate food
explanation: About one drink per hour is eliminated, so after four drinks in two hours, at least two drinks (4 - 2 = 2) remain, needing at least two more hours.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 42 (Blood Alcohol Concentration)

prompt: What usually determines whether you are riding legally after drinking?
choices: A breath, blood or urine test
How sober you look and act
How many drinks you say you had
How well you can walk a straight line
explanation: It doesn't matter how sober you may look or act. A breath, blood or urine test is what usually determines whether you are riding legally or illegally.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, pp. 42-43 (Alcohol and the Law)

prompt: Which ability is affected first when you drink?
choices: Your ability to balance the motorcycle
Your ability to judge how well you are riding
Your ability to see colors clearly
Your ability to hear traffic
explanation: Your ability to judge how well you are riding is affected first. Even as you perform worse, you think you are doing better.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 43 (Minimize the Risks)

prompt: Why does alcohol lead riders to take greater and greater risks?
choices: Alcohol makes the motorcycle easier to handle
It sharpens their reflexes for a short time after drinking
They ride worse but believe they are riding better
They feel too tired to care about risks
explanation: Although you may be performing more and more poorly, you think you are doing better and better. The result is that you ride confidently, taking greater risks.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 43 (Minimize the Risks)

prompt: What is the best way to minimize the risks of drinking and riding?
choices: Drink only beer before you ride
Ride slowly on the way home
Drink coffee before getting on the motorcycle
Separate your drinking from your riding
explanation: Minimize the risks by taking steps before you drink or by choosing to totally separate the two. Separate your drinking from your riding.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 43 (Minimize the Risks)

prompt: A rider plans to set a drink limit and pace themselves so they can ride home. How does the manual view this plan?
choices: As a poor alternative at best
As a safe plan, as long as they stop at three drinks
As the best approach for experienced riders
As safe, if they wait 30 minutes after the last drink
explanation: Setting a limit or pacing yourself are poor alternatives at best. Your judgment is one of the first things alcohol affects, so you may not realize how much your skills have suffered.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 43 (Make an Intelligent Choice)

prompt: You have been drinking and have not controlled how much you drank. What should you do?
choices: Ride home slowly using back roads
Ride home but stay in the right lane
Leave the motorcycle and arrange another way home
Drink water for a while, then ride
explanation: If you haven't controlled your drinking, you must avoid riding. Leave the motorcycle so you won't be tempted, and arrange another way to get home.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 43 (Make an Intelligent Choice)

prompt: After drinking, you wait one hour per drink before riding. What can still be a problem?
choices: Your BAC will be higher than when you stopped
Your motorcycle's engine will be cold
Nothing, because all of your riding skills are fully restored
Fatiguing after-effects of the alcohol may remain
explanation: If you exceed your limit, wait until your system eliminates the alcohol and its fatiguing after-effects. Side effects of drinking may still remain after the alcohol itself is gone.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, pp. 43-44 (Make an Intelligent Choice)

prompt: Why is it up to others to step in when a friend has had too much to drink?
choices: Friends are legally required to stop them
Someone who has had too much can't decide responsibly
The friend will always thank you for stepping in right away
Police will not stop a rider who seems fine
explanation: People who have had too much to drink are unable to make a responsible decision, so others must step in. You are rarely thanked at the time, but the alternatives are often worse.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 43 (Step In to Protect a Friend)

prompt: Which is one of the ways the manual suggests to keep a friend who has been drinking from riding?
choices: Let them ride if they promise to go slowly
Serve them food and coffee and take their key if you can
Follow behind them to make sure they get home
Let them ride if they wait 15 minutes after the last drink
explanation: Keep them there: use any excuse to keep them off the motorcycle, serve food and coffee to pass the time, explain your concerns, and take their key and secure their bike if you can.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, pp. 43-44 (Step In to Protect a Friend)

prompt: What does "get friends involved" mean when stopping someone from riding after drinking?
choices: Use peer pressure from a group of friends to intervene
Ask friends to ride alongside the rider
Have friends buy the rider one last drink
Leave the decision to whoever arrived with them
explanation: One way to protect a friend is to get other friends involved, using peer pressure from the group to intervene.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 44 (Step In to Protect a Friend)

prompt: How does cannabis tend to affect a rider?
choices: It distorts your perception of time, space and speed
It improves your focus in complex, fast-changing traffic situations
It affects only your hearing, not your vision
It has no effect once you are used to it
explanation: Cannabis tends to distort perception of time, space and speed, which is especially critical for riders who must make split-second decisions.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 44 (Cannabis & Motorcycle Operation)

prompt: How do the effects of eaten cannabis compare with smoked cannabis?
choices: They begin within minutes and fade within 2 hours
They start faster and wear off faster than when cannabis is smoked
They are identical in timing to smoked cannabis
Onset can take over an hour, and effects can last over 6 hours
explanation: Smoked cannabis usually takes effect within a few minutes and lasts 2 to 4 hours. Eaten cannabis can take more than an hour to start and last more than 6 hours.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 44 (Cannabis & Motorcycle Operation)

prompt: How does riding a motorcycle compare with driving a car in terms of fatigue?
choices: Riding is less tiring because the trip feels shorter
They are equally tiring on long trips
Riding is more tiring, so you will tire sooner
Riding is only more tiring in hot weather
explanation: Riding a motorcycle is more tiring than driving a car. On a long trip, you will tire sooner than you would in a car.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 44 (Fatigue)

prompt: According to the manual, how far do experienced riders seldom try to ride in a day?
choices: More than about two hours
More than about six hours
More than about ten hours
More than about 300 miles
explanation: To limit fatigue, limit your distance: experienced riders seldom try to ride more than about six hours a day.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 44 (Fatigue)

prompt: To fight fatigue on a long ride, how often should you stop and get off the motorcycle?
choices: At least every four hours
Only when you need fuel
At least every six hours
At least every two hours
explanation: Take frequent rest breaks: stop and get off the motorcycle at least every two hours.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 44 (Fatigue)

prompt: What does the manual recommend for protecting yourself from the elements on long rides?
choices: Ride faster to shorten your time in the wind
Dress warmly and consider a windshield
Wear lighter clothing to avoid overheating
Open your face shield for fresh air
explanation: Wind, cold and rain make you tire quickly. Dress warmly; a windshield is worth its cost if you plan to ride long distances.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 44 (Fatigue)

prompt: A rider uses an artificial stimulant to stay alert on a long trip. What often happens when it wears off?
choices: A steady return to normal alertness
Extreme fatigue or depression
Improved focus for several more hours
Only mild hunger and thirst
explanation: Artificial stimulants often result in extreme fatigue or depression when they wear off, leaving riders unable to concentrate.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 44 (Fatigue)
